Welcome toTwo Einstein Solids

Two solids in an insulated box share a fixed stock of quanta — how?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: two Einstein solids exchanging quanta at random

Source

Concept
Two Einstein solids, A and B, in thermal contact inside an insulated box, separated by a rigid wall that passes energy only. Each solid is a set of identical oscillators of angular frequency ω holding whole quanta ħω; 𝒩 is its number of oscillators (𝒩 = 3N for N atoms) and q its number of quanta. The pair is isolated, so Q = qA + qB is fixed.
Serves
Reasoning about thermal contact from the counting of microstates, with the multiplicity Ω = (q + 𝒩 − 1)!/(q!(𝒩 − 1)!), S = kB ln Ω and the statistical definition of temperature 1/T = ∂S/∂E.
Inquiry
Five questions: the direction of the average drift at the default setting, where qA ends up, how the two counting temperatures evolve, and two further starting settings. A closing card sums up what sets the direction of flow.
Misconception
Addressed through the answer choices; each choice has its own feedback, shown once it is picked.
Measured
Hop rule: an oscillator is picked at random from all 𝒩A + 𝒩B; if it holds a quantum, one moves to a second oscillator picked at random from all of them. Run makes 2 attempts per oscillator per second at 1×; one sweep = 𝒩A + 𝒩B attempts, one chart point per sweep. Step makes attempts until one quantum changes oscillator and marks that hop with a curved arrow for one second. Counting temperature T = (ħω/kB)/ln(1 + 𝒩/q), with ħω = 1.380649 × 10−21 J and kB = 1.380649 × 10−23 J K−1, so ħω/kB = 100 K; T = 0 K when q = 0. A column draws at most 24 quanta; a chevron marks a column holding more. Moving a slider or pressing Reset pauses, deals the quanta out evenly afresh and clears the chart.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honours it
Commit, then checkEach card asks for a committed choice; every card opens on a fresh, paused deal, so no outcome is on screen before the choice.
Expert deckFive questions in order, each choice with feedback aimed at its own misconception, then a closing summary.
Operational quantitiesqA, qB, the quanta per oscillator, TA, TB and sweeps are read live in the Readouts panel, from the current counts, never averaged.
Stable scaleQuantum height and column width depend on the canvas, never on the setting; the chart axes are fixed at 0–700 K and a 120-sweep window.
No planted hintsNo guide line, label or shading is drawn on the chart or in the box; every feature of the traces is left for the student to find.
Neutral colouringAll quanta share one colour, so nothing marks either solid as hot or cold.
Invariant made visibleThe scene title states that Q = qA + qB is fixed; the readouts let the student check it at any moment.
Two Einstein Solids Sharing Quanta
✦Teach me
Two Einstein solids in an insulated box Q = qA + qB fixed
Counting temperatures TA TB · ħω/kB = 100 K · 1 sweep = 𝒩A + 𝒩B attempted hops

Guided Inquiry

1 · Which way the quanta move

Keep the default setting: solid A has 10 oscillators holding 40 quanta and solid B has 90 oscillators holding 60 quanta, so B holds more energy. Which way do quanta move on average when you press ▶ Play?

2 · Where qA ends up

Press ▶ Play and watch qA in the Readouts panel. Where does qA end up?

3 · The two temperatures

The quanta have been dealt afresh at the default setting. Press ▶ Play and watch the two traces in the chart. TA starts at 448 K and TB at 109 K. What happens to the two temperatures?

4 · Equal energies

Set solid A to 10 oscillators holding 30 quanta and solid B to 90 oscillators holding 30 quanta, so the two solids start with equal energies. What happens when you press ▶ Play?

5 · Energy in proportion

Set solid A to 10 oscillators holding 10 quanta and solid B to 90 oscillators holding 90 quanta, so that B holds nine times as much energy as A. What happens when you press ▶ Play?

6 · What sets the direction of flow

Quanta drift from the solid with the higher temperature to the one with the lower, until the two temperatures are equal. That share is the most probable one, the one with the most ways ΩAΩB of arranging the quanta, and it gives every oscillator about the same number of quanta on average.

So equilibrium means equal temperatures, not equal energies: a large solid can hold far more energy than a small one at the same temperature. The hops never stop, but once the temperatures match, quanta cross the wall equally often both ways.

The Physics

Two Einstein Solids Sharing Quanta · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Two small solids share a fixed pile of energy by random hops. This sim counts each solid’s temperature from the quanta it holds and shows how the pile ends up divided between them.

What you'll learn

  • How a solid’s temperature is counted from its oscillators and its quanta.
  • What decides which way quanta drift when two solids touch.
  • How the pile is divided at equilibrium, and what is equal there.
The set-up: two solids of oscillators, a wall that passes quanta, and an isolated box.

What's on screen

  • Top scene: the oscillator columns of solid A (left) and solid B (right) with the wall between. Each dot is one quantum.
  • Bottom left: Counting temperatures, TA and TB against time in sweeps, one point per sweep. In Guided Inquiry some of this stays hidden until you answer the card.
  • Bottom right: Ways to share, the probability of each qA with a bar for the share of sweeps spent there and a marker at the current value.
  • Readouts: q, quanta per oscillator and T for each solid, the total Q and the sweeps.
See itPress Play at the opening settings and watch the columns, the chart and the readouts together. Watch for: dots hopping between the columns, the sweep count rising, and the chart gaining one point per sweep.

03

Temperature is counted from the multiplicity of the quanta

A solid is 𝒩 oscillators sharing q quanta of ħω. The number of ways to deal the quanta out is its multiplicity Ω (5.37). The notes write 3N for 𝒩, three oscillators per atom.

Notes (5.37): counting dots and dividers.

One more quantum multiplies Ω by (q + 𝒩)/(q + 1). The temperature measures that growth: the derivative of ln Ω is ln(1 + 𝒩/q) (5.39), and 1/T is that derivative divided by ħω/kB (5.40).

Notes (5.40). The sim reads T from this.

With ħω/kB = 100 K, T = (100 K)/ln(1 + 𝒩/q). It depends only on q/𝒩, the quanta per oscillator: half a quantum gives 91 K, two give 247 K, and q = 0 gives T = 0.

T against quanta per oscillator. Marks: 0.5, 2 and 4.
See itSet solid A to 10 oscillators with 5 quanta and solid B to 10 oscillators with 30, without pressing Play. Watch for: quanta per oscillator 0.50 and 3.00 in the Readouts, and the temperatures 91 K and 348 K that go with them.
04

A holds fewer quanta than B and is still the hotter solid

At the opening, A has 10 oscillators holding 40 quanta, and B has 90 oscillators holding 60. B holds more quanta in total. Per oscillator it is the other way round: A has 40/10 = 4.00 and B has 60/90 = 0.67, so each oscillator of A holds six times as many.

The temperature follows quanta per oscillator, not the total. From (5.40), TA = (100 K)/ln(1 + 10/40) = 448 K and TB = (100 K)/ln(1 + 90/60) = 109 K. B spreads its quanta over nine times as many oscillators.

The opening settings, compared three ways.
See itReset to the opening settings, without pressing Play. Watch for: A with the smaller quanta total but the larger quanta per oscillator and temperature in the Readouts.
05

A hop toward the colder solid multiplies the number of ways

Every microstate of the pair is equally likely, so the probability of a division of the quanta is proportional to the number of microstates behind it (4.20).

Notes (4.20), with Q the fixed total of quanta.

A hop moving one quantum from A to B multiplies ΩA by 40/49 = 0.816 and ΩB by 150/61 = 2.46. The product is 2.01: the new division has about twice as many microstates. The reverse hop multiplies the product by 0.50.

The flat curve of A gives up little, and the steep curve of B gains a lot. Random hops therefore drift toward the larger ΩAΩB: quanta leave the hotter solid and enter the colder one, whatever the totals are.

ln Ω against q for each solid. Dashed: the slope at the opening point.
See itPress Play at the opening settings and watch qA and qB. Watch for: qA falling while qB rises, quickly at first: after about 10 sweeps qA has dropped from 40 to about 15 on average.
06

The most probable division has equal temperatures

The drift stops where ΩAΩB is largest. There, one more quantum in A gains as much in ln Ω as it costs in B (4.25), so the two temperatures are equal.

Notes (4.25), with U = qħω.

Equal temperatures mean equal ln(1 + 𝒩/q), so equal quanta per oscillator. The quanta are shared in proportion to the oscillators, qA = Q𝒩A/(𝒩A + 𝒩B) = 100 × 10/100 = 10. The notes find the same proportional share for power-law multiplicities (4.21).

At qA = 10 and qB = 90 both solids hold one quantum per oscillator and sit at 144 K. The opening value qA = 40 is about 7×105 times less likely than the peak, and qA wanders about the peak by ±4.

P(qA) = ΩAΩB/Ωtotal for the opening pair, Q = 100.
See itPress Play at the opening settings and wait for the histogram bars to fill in. Watch for: the orange marker on Ways to share moving from 40 to the peak near 10, and both temperatures reading close to 144 K.
07

Equal energy is not equilibrium

Give both solids 30 quanta, the same energy. Solid A has 10 oscillators, so TA = 348 K, while solid B has 90 and TB = 72 K. Equal energies do not give equal temperatures.

The pair is not at the peak, which is at qA = 60 × 10/100 = 6. Quanta drift from A to B until qA is near 6 and qB near 54, 0.6 quanta per oscillator in each, at 102 K.

Temperatures at the start and, dashed, after the drift.

Start the pair at 10 quanta in A and 90 in B instead, one per oscillator on both sides. Both read 144 K, and nothing drifts on average: qA just jiggles about 10. What is shared out evenly is the quanta per oscillator.

See itSet solid A to 10 oscillators with 30 quanta and solid B to 90 with 30, then press Play. Watch for: qA falling from 30 to about 6 on average, and the two temperatures meeting near 102 K.
08

Where it matters

  • Small against large. The final temperature is set by the total quanta per oscillator, Q/(𝒩A + 𝒩B). A small solid barely moves a large one, so the pair ends nearer the large solid’s start: 144 K here, against 109 K for B and 448 K for A.
  • The peak sharpens with size. Its width goes as 1/√𝒩 (4.24). The opening pair has qA = 10 ± 4.2, a 42% spread. Two solids of 100 oscillators sharing 120 quanta have 60 ± 6.9, 11.5%. For a mole of atoms the spread is about 10−12.
  • Entropy. With S = kB ln Ω (4.26), the equal-slope condition (4.25) says ∂S/∂U is equal in both solids, and the drift is a drift toward larger total entropy.
Go deeper: the histogram peaks at 9, the average is 10

The average of qA is exactly 10, since all oscillators are equivalent. The exact distribution is a little skewed, with its tallest bar at 9 (probability 0.097, against 0.093 at 10). The proportional share is the large-number position of the peak. With 10 oscillators in A, qA also reaches 0 about once in 1369 sweeps.

09

Summary

In one line. The sim counts each solid’s temperature from its quanta and oscillators, and lets random hops show how two solids share a fixed supply of energy.

Key points

  • T = (ħω/kB)/ln(1 + 𝒩/q) depends on quanta per oscillator, not on the total.
  • Random hops drift toward the larger ΩAΩB, which sends quanta from the hotter solid to the colder one.
  • At equilibrium the temperatures, and so the quanta per oscillator, are equal: qA = Q𝒩A/(𝒩A + 𝒩B), with fluctuation of order 1/√𝒩.

Common mix-ups

  • “The solid with more quanta is the hotter one.” B holds 60 and A holds 40, yet A is at 448 K and B at 109 K.
  • “They settle at 50 quanta each.” Equal energy leaves unequal temperatures; qA settles near 10.
  • “A small solid cannot warm a large one.” A’s 40 quanta flow into B, which already holds 60, until both are near 144 K.
  • “At equilibrium the hops stop.” They go on; only the average qA stops changing.

Things to try on your own

  • Set qA = 0 and press Step: TA reads 0 K and a quantum can only enter A.
  • Give both solids 50 oscillators and 30 quanta each, then press Play.
  • Set 𝒩B = 100 and check that the final temperature moves toward B’s starting value.
